# 2 Kings Chapter 16 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 237r–237v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_016_page_472.jpg, 2KI_016_page_473.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham king of Judah began to reign.

**2** Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God, as David his father had done.

**3** He walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even passed his son through the fire, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD had driven out before the people of Israel.

**4** He sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.

**5** Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war. They besieged Ahaz but could not overpower him.

**6** At that time Rezin king of Aram recovered Elath for Aram and drove the Judeans from Elath, and the Arameans came to Elath and settled there to this day.

**7** So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, saying, "I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hand of the king of Aram and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen against me."

**8** Ahaz took the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the king's palace, and sent them as a gift to the king of Assyria.

**9** The king of Assyria listened to him. He went up against Damascus and captured it, carrying its people captive to Kir, and he put Rezin to death.

**10** When King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw the altar at Damascus. King Ahaz sent to Uriah the priest a sketch of the altar and a detailed plan of its construction.

**11** Uriah the priest built the altar in accordance with all that King Ahaz had sent from Damascus. He finished it before King Ahaz returned.

**12** When the king came from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached the altar and went up on it.

**13** He burned his burnt offering and his grain offering, poured out his drink offering, and dashed the blood of his peace offerings against the altar.

**14** The bronze altar that stood before the LORD he moved from the front of the house — from between his new altar and the house of the LORD — and placed it on the north side of his altar.

**15** Then King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest: "On the great altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering, the king's burnt offering and his grain offering, and the burnt offering of all the people of the land with their grain offering and their drink offerings. Dash against it all the blood of burnt offerings and all the blood of sacrifices. But the bronze altar shall be mine for inquiry."

**16** Uriah the priest did everything King Ahaz commanded.

**17** King Ahaz cut off the frames of the stands and removed the basins from them. He took down the Sea from the bronze oxen that supported it and set it on a stone pavement.

**18** The covered Sabbath walkway that had been built at the temple, and the king's outer entrance, he removed from the house of the LORD — because of the king of Assyria.

**19** Now the rest of the acts of Ahaz, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

**20** Ahaz lay down with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. And Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Ahaz is the anti-David and the anti-Moses in a single portrait. His reign is narrated as a systematic dismantling of everything that made Judah distinct: he practices child sacrifice (v.3), empties the temple treasury for a foreign king (v.8), copies a pagan altar with the vocabulary of sacred architecture (v.10), displaces YHWH's altar (v.14), and strips Solomon's temple furnishings (vv.17-18). The phrase "because of the king of Assyria" (v.18) is the chapter's theological verdict: Ahaz has replaced YHWH with Tiglath-pileser. His self-designation as Assyria's "servant and son" (v.7) completes the betrayal — covenant language redirected to an empire. The chapter sets the stage for Hezekiah, who will undo his father's work.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.3 — "passed his son through the fire" vs. "sacrificed his own son in the fire"
- **EMET:** "his-son he-passed-through the-fire [he'evir ba-esh]"
- **LOGOS:** "passed his son through the fire"
- **PNEUMA:** "sacrificed his own son in the fire"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "passed his son through the fire" — the Hebrew uses the technical phrase *he'evir ba-esh*, which should be preserved. While PNEUMA's interpretation is correct, the traditional phrasing maintains the biblical idiom.

### V.8 — "bribe" vs. "gift" vs. "payment"
- **EMET:** "a-bribe [shochad]"
- **LOGOS:** "a gift"
- **PNEUMA:** "a payment"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "a gift" — the Hebrew *shochad* can mean bribe, gift, or tribute. "Gift" is neutral enough to carry the diplomatic context while allowing the reader to perceive the moral dimension.

### V.15 — "to inquire" vs. "for inquiry" vs. "for seeking guidance"
- **EMET:** "to-inquire [levaqer]"
- **LOGOS:** "to use for inquiry"
- **PNEUMA:** "for seeking guidance"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "for inquiry" — preserves the ambiguity of *levaqer* (which may mean inspect, inquire, or divine) without importing too specific an interpretation.

### V.18 — "turned" vs. "redirected" vs. "dismantled/removed"
- **EMET:** "he-turned [hesev]"
- **LOGOS:** "he redirected these away"
- **PNEUMA:** "dismantled... removing them"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "he removed from the house of the LORD" — *hesev* means to turn away or divert. "Removed" captures the result without overstating the method.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
